⏺ Based on the CLAUDE.md and what I found in the code:

  Phase 3 hasn't started. The current frontend has hardcoded placeholder data —
  only 5 fake mixes (IDs 043–047) in a TX array inside sections2.jsx, with dummy
   audio URLs and fabricated dates. The scenes section is similarly hardcoded.

  Here's what Phase 3 requires, in order:

  1. ARCHIVE section — replace the hardcoded TX array with a
  fetch('/public/assets/metadata/mixes.json') call, then map the JSON fields
  (title, slug, duration, releaseDate, mood, views, audioPath, youtubeUrl,
  soundcloudUrl) to the existing archive row components. All 94 mixes instead
  of 5.
  2. SCENES section — same pattern with scenes.json, mapping name, slug, type,
  description, episodeNumber, mood, videoPath, thumbnailPath to the scene cards.
  3. Mood tags / sort / filter — the mood field from both JSONs drives the mood
  chip/badge displayed on each card. The archive already has a sort UI (NEWEST,
  OLDEST, A-Z, POPULAR) that needs to work against real data.
  4. YT / SC links — youtubeUrl and soundcloudUrl wire up to the existing
  external link buttons. 22 mixes have null soundcloudUrl, so those SC buttons
  need to hide gracefully.

  The blocker to discuss before writing any code: the app is currently a Claude 
  Artifact bundled file (all JS embedded as base64 in index.html). To do Phase 3
   properly — with a real fetch() call to the local JSON — the site needs to be
  served (not opened as a file:// URL), and the JS source files need to be
  editable outside the bundle. Do you want to unbundle the app into plain
  separate files first, or work within the current bundled structure?

❯ how do i view my website because the index.html doesn;t work now?             

⏺ The site now uses fetch() to load the JSON data, so it needs to be served over
   HTTP — opening index.html directly as a file won't work anymore.

  Since you have Python 3, just run this from the project folder:

  python3 -m http.server 3000

  Then open http://localhost:3000 in your browser.

  To stop it, press Ctrl+C in the terminal.

  You can also run it in the background with ! in this prompt if you want:
  python3 -m http.server 3000

✻ Churned for 9s

❯ How is music playing on my website now without a backend?                     

⏺ It's just static file serving — no backend logic involved.

  Here's what happens when you press play:

  1. app.js builds the audio source path from mixes.json: audioSrc = '/' + 
  m.audioPath → e.g. /public/assets/mixes/audio/lo-fi-house-mix-retrospect.mp3
  2. The <audio> element in the React app sets audio.src to that path and calls
  audio.play()
  3. The browser requests that file from
  http://localhost:3000/public/assets/mixes/audio/...
  4. Python's http.server sees the request and just sends back the .mp3 file
  from your disk
  5. The browser plays it with its built-in audio decoder

  Python's http.server is essentially acting as a dumb file cabinet — no
  business logic, just "someone asked for a file, here it is." The browser
  handles all the actual audio decoding and playback itself.

  This breaks the moment you deploy, because the MP3s are gitignored and won't
  be on the server. That's exactly why Phase 7 exists — moving the audio files
  to Cloudflare R2 so they have a real URL independent of your local disk.

  Current context:                                                              
                                                                                
  * Mix data comes from `mixes.json`.                                           
  * Audio playback is handled through the React `<audio>` element.              
  * Archive sorting currently supports newest, oldest, A–Z, and popular.        
  * Archive and Scenes sections use terminal-style pagination/signals.          
                                                                                
  1. Archive sorting should not interrupt the current mix                       
                                                                                
  In the Archive section, sorting the track list between newest, oldest, A–Z,   
  and popular should not affect the currently selected or currently playing     
  mix.                                                                          
                                                                                
  Current issue:                                                                
                                                                                
  * When I click a sort option, the music stops playing or resets.              
                                                                                
  Expected behavior:                                                            
                                                                                
  * Sorting should only change the visible order of the archive track list.     
  * Sorting should not stop, pause, reload, reset, or replace the current       
  audio.                                                                        
  * Do not call `audio.pause()`, `audio.load()`, or change `audio.src` unless   
  the user explicitly clicks a different mix.                                   
  * Preserve the current playing/paused state, current timestamp, selected mix, 
   and volume.                                                                  
  * If needed, separate the current mix state from the sorted archive list      
  state.                                                                        
  * Make sure React list keys are stable and based on the mix slug/id, not the  
  array index.                                                                  
                                                                                
  2. Make archive volume/output indicators vertical and better positioned       
                                                                                
  In the Archive section, the volume/output indicator should be vertical in all 
   places where it appears.                                                     
                                                                                
  Current issue:                                                                
                                                                                
  * The volume indicator feels out of place.                                    
  * It appears positioned in a way that does not visually connect to the        
  waveform.                                                                     
  * In some areas, it feels like the user may need to scroll horizontally.      
                                                                                
  Expected behavior:                                                            
                                                                                
  * Make the OUTPUT/volume indicator vertical in the archive current-player     
  area.                                                                         
  * Reposition it closer to the waveform box so it feels connected to the audio 
   visualization.                                                               
  * A good layout would be: waveform preview on the left, vertical OUTPUT meter 
   directly beside it or in a compact block near it.                            
  * Do not make users scroll horizontally to see or interact with it.           
  * Keep the CRT green bar style.                                               
  * The visual bars should reflect the current website audio volume.            
  * If interactive, the control should update the HTMLAudioElement volume       
  between `0` and `1`.                                                          
  * Make sure the archive table OUTPUT column also keeps a clean vertical-bar   
  style and remains aligned.                                                    
                                                                                
  3. Move the archive current-player date                                       
                                                                                
  In the Archive current-player panel, the date currently appears underneath    
  the LISTEN/PAUSE button and looks out of place.                               
                                                                                
  Please reposition the date somewhere more logical.                            
                                                                                
  Preferred direction:                                                          
                                                                                
  * Treat the date as metadata, not as a control.                               
  * Place it near the mix ID/slug metadata line, or in a small metadata row     
  with runtime/duration.                                                        
  * It should not sit directly under the LISTEN/PAUSE button.                   
  * Keep the date visually dimmer than the title and controls.                  
  * Make the layout feel intentional on desktop and responsive on smaller       
  screens.                                                                      
                                                                                
  4. Archive pagination should show 5 mixes per signal/page                     
                                                                                
  In the Archive section, only display 5 mixes per signal/page.                 
                                                                                
  Expected behavior:                                                            
                                                                                
  * Each archive page displays exactly 5 mixes, except the final page if fewer

  * Use the existing terminal-style pagination controls.                        
  * Page count should be calculated dynamically from `mixes.json`.              
  * Sorting should reset the archive list to page 1.                            
  * Sorting should not affect the current playing mix.

  * Each Scenes page displays exactly 6 scene cards, except the final page if

✻ Worked for 1m 8s

❯ Was all of this prompting front-end design?                                   

⏺ Yes, everything we've done is 100% front-end — no server, no database, no
  backend of any kind.

  Here's a breakdown of what it all is:

  Static files served by Python's built-in HTTP server:
  - index.html — entry point
  - css/styles.css — all styling
  - js/*.js — React app, components, logic

  Data layer: Two JSON files (mixes.json, scenes.json) that the browser fetches
  and renders directly. No API, no queries.

  "Backend" equivalent: python3 -m http.server 3000 — this is just a dumb file
  server. It serves any file you ask for, no logic whatsoever. Any web server
  (Nginx, Apache, Cloudflare Pages) could replace it.

  localStorage — browser storage, entirely client-side. Nothing touches a
  server.

  ---
  The roadmap phases that are still ahead are where the real backend work
  begins:

  ┌───────┬────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Phase │                    What it actually is                     │
  ├───────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ 4     │ FastAPI — Python web server with real API endpoints        │
  ├───────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ 5     │ PostgreSQL — actual database replacing the JSON files      │
  ├───────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ 6     │ Railway deployment — hosting the backend + DB in the cloud │
  ├───────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ 7     │ Cloudflare R2 — object storage for the audio/video files   │
  └───────┴────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Right now the site is essentially a static website — everything runs in the
  browser, nothing runs on a server.

✻ Worked for 10s

❯ what's next for Phase 4?                                                      

⏺ Based on the CLAUDE.md roadmap, Phase 4 is building a FastAPI backend with
  these endpoints:

  GET /api/mixes
  GET /api/mixes/latest
  GET /api/scenes
  GET /api/scenes?page=1
  GET /api/scenes?tag=rainy

  Practically, here's the order I'd recommend:

  1. Set up the FastAPI project
  - Create backend/ directory with main.py, requirements.txt
  - Install FastAPI + Uvicorn
  - Add CORS so the frontend (on port 3000) can talk to the API (on a different
  port)

  2. Wire up the JSON files first
  - Have FastAPI read mixes.json and scenes.json from disk initially
  - Swap zero front-end code — the API just becomes the new source of truth
  - The frontend fetches from /api/mixes instead of the JSON file directly

  3. Update the frontend fetch calls
  - In app.js, change the two fetch() calls from the JSON paths to the API URLs
  - That's the only front-end change needed

  4. Add the useful endpoints
  - /api/mixes/latest — returns the newest mix (used by the ticker)
  - /api/scenes?page=1 — server-side pagination (replaces the current
  client-side TermPageBar slicing)
  - Mood/tag filtering when ready

  5. Test locally with both servers running
  - Frontend: python3 -m http.server 3000
  - Backend: uvicorn main:app --reload --port 8000

  ---
  The big question before starting: do you want to skip directly to Phase 5
  (PostgreSQL) and build the API against the database from the start, or build
  it against the JSON files first and swap later?

  Reading from JSON is faster to get running, and Phase 5 just replaces the data
   source inside FastAPI — the API endpoints and the frontend stay identical
  either way.

❯ Before starting Phae 4, what is a creative way for the .mp4 clips to play on  
  the website that fits with the theme? Maybe some sort of web player box       
  playing the video that can be enlarged?                                       

⏺ Given the ARCHIVE.SYS / CRT / wired aesthetic, here are a few concepts that
  would fit well:

  ---
  Option A — "Active Signal Feed" panel (most cohesive)

  When a scene card is selected, a panel slides in or expands below the scene
  grid — styled like a surveillance/broadcast monitor:

  ┌─ SIGNAL FEED ──────────────────── ◉ TRANSMITTING ─┐
  │                                                     │
  │   [video plays here with CRT scanlines overlay]    │
  │                                                     │
  │  ▸ PAUSE   00:14 / 01:32   ░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░   │
  │  EPISODE 03 · CLIP 07 · BEDROOM STATIC             │
  └─────────────────────────── ⊞ EXPAND SIGNAL ────────┘

  Clicking EXPAND SIGNAL opens it to a larger centered modal/overlay with the
  same CRT styling but filling more of the screen.

  ---
  Option B — Expanding card in-place

  The selected scene card expands vertically (like the archive active row does)
  to reveal the video player embedded within the card itself. No separate panel
  — the card just grows to fit the video. Feels like "tuning into" that signal.

  ---
  Option C — Fixed corner "Transmission Window"

  A small fixed-position CRT monitor in the bottom-right corner (like the hero
  mini-player but for video). Plays whichever scene is selected. A single click
  enlarges it to a centered overlay. Stays visible as you scroll.

  ---
  My recommendation: Option A

  It matches the archive's active-row pattern — selecting a scene "activates" a
  feed below, with the option to go full-screen. The expand interaction gives
  users control without forcing an overlay. It also reuses the visual language
  already established (the active player panel in the archive section).

  ---
  Implementation would need:
  - A <video> element (HTML5, no library needed)
  - videoPath from scenes.json — already in the data
  - The thumbnail already loads, so the video src is just swapping .jpg → .mp4
  path prefix
  - CRT scanlines overlay (already used in the Oscilloscope — same CSS pattern)
  - Show/hide logic tied to the existing selected state in SceneGrid

  Want me to build Option A?

❯ Would this be back-end design?                                                

⏺ No, this is still 100% front-end.

  The .mp4 files already live on your disk at:
  public/assets/scenes/videos/episode-XX_clip-NN.mp4

  And scenes.json already has the videoPath for every clip. The browser's
  built-in <video> element handles all playback natively — same way the <audio>
  element plays your mixes right now, no backend needed.

  // Already in scenes.json, ready to use:
  "videoPath": "public/assets/scenes/videos/episode-01_clip-01.mp4"

  Python's http.server just serves the file when the browser asks for it — same
  as it does for the MP3s.

  ---
  The only thing that becomes a backend concern later is when the files move to
  Cloudflare R2 (Phase 7) — at that point the videoPath changes from a local
  path to a CDN URL like
  https://media.weebtrax.com/scenes/episode-01_clip-01.mp4. The player code
  stays identical, just the URL changes.

  ---
  So the full video player — styled panel, CRT overlay, expand/collapse,
  controls, everything — is purely front-end React work. Want me to build it?

⏺ Video player is live. Now for your now-playing question:

  ---
  The OBS Spotify overlay is a floating "lower third" — it shows the track name,
   scrolling if long, with a thin progress bar. All front-end, no backend needed
   since your app already has the current mix title, elapsed time, and progress
  in React state.

  The best fit for the WeebTrax aesthetic is a fixed broadcast bar at the very 
  bottom of the screen — visible everywhere on the site while music plays, fades
   out on standby:

  ◉ ON AIR  ──────────────────────  Lo-Fi House Mix | Euphoric Sounds For Your
  Inner Youth  ──  00:39:26

  It would:
  - Appear only when a mix is actively playing (fade out on pause/standby)
  - Show the current mix title with a slow-scrolling marquee if it's long
  - Have a thin green progress line along the very bottom edge
  - Stay fixed as the user scrolls through any section
  - Fit in with the "ARCHIVE.SYS · STATUS: ONLINE" terminal broadcast feel

  Alternatively, for the archive section specifically (the image you shared), I
  could add a "NOW DECODING" label that marquee-scrolls the current mix title
  directly in the top status bar of the active player — replacing the static ◎ 
  STANDBY text.

  My recommendation: the fixed bottom broadcast bar. It mimics OBS exactly
  (always visible, non-intrusive), works across the whole site, and fits the
  live transmission theme. Want me to build it?

❯ How would I be able to display the track I.D. for each song playing in the    
  mix rather than displaying the mix itself? WOuld I need another dictionary    
  within the mixes.json?                                                        

⏺ Good question — yes, you'd need a tracklist added to the data. Here's how it
  would work:

  ---
  The data problem:

  Each mix is a continuous DJ set — one long MP3 with many individual songs
  blended together. Right now mixes.json only knows the mix as a whole, not
  what's playing inside it at any given second.

  To show the current track, you need timestamps that map positions in the mix
  to track names:

  {
    "id": "mix-001",
    "title": "Lo-Fi House Mix | Retrospect",
    "duration": "00:45:18",
    "tracklist": [
      { "time": "00:00:00", "artist": "Floating Points", "title": "LesAlpx" },
      { "time": "00:04:32", "artist": "Motor City Drum Ensemble", "title": "Raw 
  Cuts #7" },
      { "time": "00:09:15", "artist": "Unknown", "title": "Untitled" }
    ]
  }

  The frontend then reads audio.currentTime, finds which timestamp range it
  falls into, and displays that track.

  ---
  To answer your question directly — yes, a nested array in mixes.json is the 
  right approach. No separate file needed unless the tracklists get very long.

  ---
  The bigger practical question:

  Do you actually have the tracklists for your 94 mixes? There are three ways to
   get them:

  ┌─────────────────────────────────┬────────┬─────────────────────────────┐
  │             Method              │ Effort │          Accuracy           │
  ├─────────────────────────────────┼────────┼─────────────────────────────┤
  │ Manual — timestamp each track   │ High   │ Perfect                     │
  │ yourself from the mix           │        │                             │
  ├─────────────────────────────────┼────────┼─────────────────────────────┤
  │ YouTube description — copy      │        │                             │
  │ tracklists from video           │ Medium │ Good                        │
  │ descriptions if they exist      │        │                             │
  ├─────────────────────────────────┼────────┼─────────────────────────────┤
  │ ACRCloud / Shazam API —         │ Low    │ ~70–80% (misses             │
  │ auto-detect tracks by audio     │ setup  │ unreleased/white-label)     │
  │ fingerprinting                  │        │                             │
  └─────────────────────────────────┴────────┴─────────────────────────────┘

  Lo-fi house mixes often include unreleased or white-label tracks that
  fingerprinting won't catch, so manual is usually most accurate.

  ---
  Worth noting for Phase 4/5:

  This naturally becomes a tracks table in PostgreSQL when you get there:

  tracks (id, mix_id, timestamp_secs, artist, title)

  For now the nested tracklist array in mixes.json is the right front-end-only
  approach. Do you have the tracklists available for any of the mixes?

⏺ Fixed. The bug was that getMixes() explicitly listed every field it kept from
  the raw JSON — id, title, slug, etc. — and tracklist was never in that list,
  so it got silently dropped. Adding tracklist: m.tracklist || [] passes it
  through.

  and updates automatically as playback crosses each timestamp in the tracklist.
